keep: The idea is named up front: A⁻¹ plays A backwards, A then A⁻¹ leaves every point alone, and it exists only when the determinant is not zero.
The recipe is earned before it is named: [2 −1; −4 3] times A gives [2 0; 0 2], 2 times I, with 2 the determinant, then the general (ad − bc) I, then divide.

The zero-determinant case shows both endings from the brief: a dot off the line gets no point, a dot on it gets a whole line of points (x + y = 2), after the starting point races from (1, 1) to (−8, 10) as the determinant falls 1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1.

Each brief mistake has its own puzzle and hint: 1 ÷ each entry (screen 4, multiply back gives 5 not 1), which cannot be undone with a negative determinant as the trap (screen 8), forwards instead of backwards (screen 10), adding loop currents in the shared resistor (screen 12), the determinant added (screen 13).

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO, ending on two mixed circuit puzzles. The circuit numbers match the brief: 6I₁ − 2I₂ = 12, −2I₁ + 6I₂ = 4, determinant 32, 2.5 A, 1.5 A and 1 A shared. Four footnotes, one per sentence, none naming a source. Validator: no problems.
fix: Causal step skipped: 'Done the other way round, AA⁻¹ is I too' is asserted. Say why: undo first, and A carries each point back from where A⁻¹ sent it.
Misconception not shown failing in explain: the 1 ÷ each entry reading is only denied. Show it failing with the number: times A it gives 5 in row 1, column 1, not 1.
False absolute: 'Lean j towards i's line and the determinant shrinks' holds for the picture's lean, not any lean. Tie it to the picture.
Causal gap: 'the recipe fails when that is 0. The picture shows why' reads as if only the recipe fails. Say that no inverse exists at all, whatever the method, and why.
False absolute in practice: 'off the diagonal is minus the shared resistance' needs both loop currents drawn the same way round.
The brief's 'and then vanishing' is only one of the two zero endings. Say 'until at 0 no single point lands there', which covers both.
Analogy breaks: 'a transformer scales one number' is loose. Say an ideal transformer scales the voltage by one fixed ratio.
